```{r}
library(evomod2)
```

The genetic architecture decides how variation is generated and inherited,
and with it how G can evolve. This vignette compares the three architectures
in evomod2 with small simulations, then shows how recombination affects G.
The simulations are short so the vignette builds quickly; the examples in
`system.file("examples", package = "evomod2")` run longer, replicated
versions.

## Three architectures

All three have diploid loci whose two alleles are added up within the locus.
They differ in what an allele is and how loci combine:

| Architecture | An allele is | Genotypic value | Mutation |
|---|---|---|---|
| `additive()` | an effect vector, one value per trait | sum over loci | `mutation()`: adds a multivariate normal vector |
| `binary_b()` | a scalar effect `y` and a 0/1 column of `B` | `B y` | `binary_b_mutation()`: changes `y`, flips entries of `B` |
| `multilinear()` | an effect vector | sum over loci plus pairwise interactions `ε(Y_i, Y_j)` | `mutation()` |

In `binary_b()` an allele affects the traits marked in its column of `B`, all
by the same amount, and `B` mutates, so the pattern of pleiotropy itself can
evolve. In `additive()` every allele affects every trait with independent
effects. `multilinear()` adds epistasis: the effect of a locus depends on the
rest of the genome.

## Pleiotropy and modularity under corridor selection

Four traits, two modules (traits 1-2 and 3-4). After stabilizing selection,
the optimum of module 1 moves (corridor selection):

```{r}
corridor <- list(
  stabilizing(1000, omega = 10),
  directional(1500, delta_theta = c(0.004, 0.004, 0, 0), omega = 10)
)
models <- list(
  binary_b = evomod_model(binary_b(loci = 50, traits = 4),
                          binary_b_mutation(rate = 0.001, sd = 0.2, rate_b = 0.0005),
                          env_sd = 0.8, init_sd = 0.2),
  additive = evomod_model(additive(loci = 50, traits = 4),
                          mutation(rate = 0.001, cov = 0.2),
                          env_sd = 0.8, init_sd = 0.2)
)
pops <- lapply(models, evolve, regimes = corridor, n = 500, record_every = 50, seed = 1)
```

Average genetic correlations within and between the modules, through time:

```{r}
module_trace <- function(pop, name) {
  G <- g_matrices(pop)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(G), function(gen) {
    a <- avg_corr(G[[gen]], modules = list(1:2, 3:4))
    data.frame(architecture = name, generation = as.integer(gen),
               within_1 = a$within[1], within_2 = a$within[2], between = a$between)
  }))
}
trace <- do.call(rbind, Map(module_trace, pops, names(pops)))

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (arch in names(pops)) {
  d <- trace[trace$architecture == arch, ]
  matplot(d$generation, d[, c("within_1", "within_2", "between")], type = "l", lty = 1,
          col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "grey50"), ylim = c(-0.2, 0.6),
          xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Average genetic correlation", main = arch)
  abline(v = 1000, col = "grey85")
}
legend("topleft", c("within module 1", "within module 2", "between"),
       col = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "grey50"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(op)
```

With a binary `B`, alleles affecting several traits create correlations, and
selection can change which traits alleles affect. (These are single
populations, so the traces are noisy.) In the additive model,
correlations only appear as selection enriches alleles whose effects on the
selected traits point the same way. `inst/examples/corridor_selection.R` runs
this comparison with 20 replicates.

## Multilinear epistasis

With multilinear epistasis the effect of an allele depends on the genetic
background. Positive directional epistasis (here `ε[1, 1, 1] > 0`) makes
substitutions in trait 1 larger as the population moves in the positive
direction, so additive variance grows under directional selection; negative
epistasis shrinks it:

```{r}
self_epistasis <- function(e) {
  E <- array(0, c(2, 2, 2))
  E[1, 1, 1] <- e
  E
}
epistasis <- c(negative = -0.05, none = 0, positive = 0.05)
selection <- list(stabilizing(1000, omega = 20),
                  directional(2000, delta_theta = c(0.005, 0), omega = 20))
G11 <- sapply(epistasis, function(e) {
  arch <- if (e == 0) additive(50, 2) else multilinear(50, 2, self_epistasis(e))
  m <- evomod_model(arch, mutation(rate = 0.005, cov = 0.05), env_sd = 1)
  pop <- evolve(m, selection, n = 500, record_every = 50, seed = 2)
  v <- variances(pop)
  v$G[v$trait == "trait1"]
})
gens <- seq(0, 3000, by = 50)   # recorded generations
matplot(gens, G11, type = "l", lty = 1, col = c("#0072B2", "grey40", "#D55E00"),
        xlab = "Generation", ylab = "Additive variance, trait 1")
abline(v = 1000, col = "grey85")
legend("topleft", names(epistasis), col = c("#0072B2", "grey40", "#D55E00"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

`local_effects()` gives the effect of each locus in the background of the
rest of the genome. After the population has moved in the positive direction
of trait 1, positive epistasis amplifies every locus effect on trait 1 (by
about `1 + ε S`, where `S` is the sum of the other locus effects), so local
effects lie on a line steeper than 1 when plotted against the reference
effects:

```{r}
m <- evomod_model(multilinear(50, 2, self_epistasis(0.05)),
                  mutation(rate = 0.005, cov = 0.05), env_sd = 1)
pop <- evolve(m, selection, n = 500, record_every = 500, seed = 2)
L <- local_effects(pop, individual = 1)
Y <- local_effects(evomod_model(additive(50, 2), mutation(0.1, 0.1)),
                   alleles = genomes(pop)[, , 1])   # reference (additive) effects
plot(Y[1, ], L[1, ], xlab = "Reference effect, trait 1", ylab = "Local effect, trait 1")
abline(0, 1, col = "grey60")
```

## Linkage and the decomposition of G

By default loci recombine freely. A genetic map places loci on chromosomes:

```{r}
linked <- evomod_model(additive(50, 4), mutation(rate = 0.001, cov = 0.2),
                       env_sd = 0.8, init_sd = 0.2,
                       recombination = genetic_map(chromosomes = 1, length = 0.5))
linked$recombination$rates[1:3]   # between neighbouring loci
```

G splits into a genic part, the G expected without linkage disequilibrium,
and the part due to linkage disequilibrium between loci. Stabilizing
selection builds negative linkage disequilibrium that hides part of the
genic variance (the Bulmer effect), much more strongly when loci are linked:

```{r}
free <- evomod_model(additive(50, 4), mutation(rate = 0.001, cov = 0.2),
                     env_sd = 0.8, init_sd = 0.2)
stab <- stabilizing(1500, omega = 5)
decomp <- sapply(list(free = free, linked = linked), function(m) {
  d <- g_decomposition(evolve(m, stab, n = 500, seed = 3))
  c(G = d$G[1, 1], genic = d$genic[1, 1], ld = d$ld[1, 1])
})
round(decomp, 3)
```

`g_matrices(pop, "genic")` and `g_matrices(pop, "ld")` give the two parts at
every recorded generation. For architectures where genotypic values are not sums of
allele effects (multilinear epistasis), the same split can be estimated by
shuffling alleles among individuals at each locus (do O & Whitlock 2023):

```{r}
m <- evomod_model(multilinear(50, 2, self_epistasis(0.05)),
                  mutation(rate = 0.005, cov = 0.05), env_sd = 1,
                  recombination = genetic_map(1, 0.5))
pop_ml <- evolve(m, selection, n = 500, seed = 4)
lapply(g_decomposition(pop_ml, method = "shuffle", shuffles = 10), round, 3)
```

## Mutational covariance

New mutations have effects that depend on the genetic background when there
is epistasis. `mutational_covariance()` applies single mutations to genomes of
the population and measures their effects. In the additive model the
covariance of the effects of one mutation is the mutational covariance of the
model (`0.05^2` here); with positive directional epistasis, after the
population moved in the positive direction of trait 1, mutations at trait 1
have larger effects, and on average positive ones:

```{r}
add <- evomod_model(additive(50, 2), mutation(rate = 0.005, cov = 0.05), env_sd = 1)
pop_add <- evolve(add, selection, n = 500, seed = 4)
mc <- list(additive = mutational_covariance(pop_add, n = 20000),
           epistatic = mutational_covariance(pop_ml, n = 20000))
sapply(mc, function(x) c(var_trait1 = x$per_mutation[1, 1], mean_trait1 = x$mean[[1]]))
``` `inst/examples/corridor_linkage.R` compares the
binary B and additive architectures under free recombination and tight
linkage.
